case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the trial court's use of a screen to block a four-year-old child witness's view of the defendant during a sexual abuse trial violated the Confrontation Clause of the Sixth Amendment by failing to make the constitutionally required case-specific finding of necessity.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Sixth Amendment Confrontation Clause (U.S. Constitution); Mississippi Code Section 99-43-101(2)(g) — a mandatory statute requiring use of a screen procedure for child witnesses in sexual abuse cases without requiring individualized judicial findings of necessity
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The trial court violated the Confrontation Clause by mechanically applying a mandatory Mississippi statute that presumed trauma to child witnesses without conducting the individualized, case-specific inquiry required by Coy v. Iowa and Maryland v. Craig. Petitioner argues this is especially egregious because the child witness (his four-year-old daughter) actually expressed love for him and showed no signs of trauma from his presence — directly contradicting any presumption of necessity. The trial judge himself expressed concern about the statute's constitutionality but felt bound by its mandatory language, which Petitioner argues is precisely the kind of legislatively imposed presumption that the Supreme Court has already rejected. Petitioner further contends summary reversal is appropriate given the clear and direct conflict with controlling Supreme Court precedent.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Mississippi state courts' rejection of the Confrontation Clause challenge should be upheld because the trial proceedings satisfied confrontation's essential elements — the witness testified under oath, was subject to cross-examination, and was observable by the jury. The State argues the trial court did make a sufficient determination that the screen procedure was necessary to protect the child witness from trauma, and that the overwhelming independent evidence of guilt — including witness testimony, statements to authorities, and a videotaped forensic interview — renders any procedural error harmless. The State further contends the case does not warrant Supreme Court review because the confrontation requirements were substantively met.
key_precedents: Coy v. Iowa, 487 U.S. 1012 (1988) — established that the Confrontation Clause guarantees a defendant the right to face-to-face confrontation with witnesses and that legislatively imposed presumptions of trauma are insufficient to override this right

Maryland v. Craig, 497 U.S. 836 (1990) — held that face-to-face confrontation may be dispensed with only where the trial court makes a case-specific, individualized finding that the procedure is necessary to protect the witness
Crawford v. Washington, 541 U.S. 36 (2004) — abrogated Ohio v. Roberts on other grounds; landmark Confrontation Clause case
Ohio v. Roberts, 448 U.S. 56 (1980) — prior Confrontation Clause standard, abrogated by Crawford
Kentucky v. Stincer, 482 U.S. 730 (1987) — addressed Confrontation Clause elements
California v. Green, 399 U.S. 157 (1970) — defined the core elements of confrontation including oath, cross-examination, and jury observation of demeanor
Chambers v. Mississippi, 410 U.S. 284 (1973) — Confrontation Clause protections
Hicks v. Miranda, 422 U.S. 332 (1975) — addressed obligation of state courts to follow controlling Supreme Court precedent
Czekala-Chatham v. State, 195 So. 3d 187 (Miss. 2015) — Mississippi Supreme Court case affirming obligation to follow U.S. Supreme Court precedent
Hall v. State (Mississippi) — struck down Mississippi's Evidence of Child Sexual Abuse Act as violating separation of powers under the Mississippi Constitution
Little v. State, 72 So. 3d 557 (Miss. Ct. App. 2011) — admissibility of forensic interviews under tender-years exception
Lambert v. State, 101 So. 3d 1172 (Miss. Ct. App. 2012) — forensic interview admissibility
Cook v. State, 161 So. 3d 1057 (Miss. 2015) — forensic interview admissibility under tender-years exception
case_analysis.legal_complexity: Complex — The case sits at the intersection of Sixth Amendment Confrontation Clause doctrine, state legislative authority to enact mandatory child-protection statutes, the constitutional requirement for individualized judicial fact-finding before departing from face-to-face testimony, harmless error analysis, and the binding nature of Supreme Court precedent on state courts. The tension between child witness protection policies and constitutional confrontation rights, combined with the mandatory versus discretionary nature of the state statute and the factual irony that the child expressed affection rather than fear toward the defendant, makes this a legally and factually nuanced case with significant implications for how states may structure child witness protection procedures.

John Roberts.reasoning: The unanimity of my colleagues across the ideological spectrum — from Justice Thomas's originalist critique to Justice Sotomayor's and Justice Kagan's more functionalist approaches — confirms that this case presents a straightforward application of Craig and Coy rather than a genuinely contested constitutional question. Justice Kavanaugh's point about institutional legitimacy resonates with me particularly: allowing Mississippi to stand as the sole outlier jurisdiction defying controlling Supreme Court precedent would undermine the Court's authority in a way that my minimalist philosophy cannot countenance, since institutional legitimacy cuts both ways — it counsels restraint when precedent is unclear, but demands enforcement when it is plain. The narrowest ground here is simply that Craig's individualized-finding requirement was not satisfied, and I would write the majority opinion to hold precisely that and no more, explicitly reserving the question of whether a properly conducted hearing on remand might support use of the screen on these specific facts. I note that the child's expressed affection for the defendant, combined with the trial judge's own constitutional doubts, makes this an unusually clean vehicle for reaffirming Craig without needing to address harder questions about the outer limits of permissible legislative accommodation of child witnesses.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: I agree with the core analysis shared by all my colleagues, including Justice Barrett's precise articulation that Maryland v. Craig requires the necessity finding to be 'case-specific' and supported by evidence heard by the trial court — a requirement Mississippi's mandatory statute structurally forecloses. I write separately to emphasize that my own position, expressed in dissent in Craig itself, is that the Confrontation Clause admits no exceptions whatsoever to face-to-face confrontation, meaning Mississippi's statute fails not merely because it lacks individualized findings but because no legislative or judicial procedure can constitutionally substitute for physical confrontation. Even accepting Craig's balancing framework on its own terms, however, the result here is identical: the mandatory statutory presumption, the trial court's expressed constitutional doubt, and the child's affirmative expression of affection for the defendant collectively make this among the clearest Confrontation Clause violations imaginable. I concur in reversal, though I would go further than Chief Justice Roberts' narrow remand approach and note that Craig itself remains vulnerable to reconsideration under the original public meaning of the Sixth Amendment.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself is telling — when Justice Thomas and Justice Sotomayor reach the same conclusion through different methodological paths, the constitutional answer is clear. Justice Thomas correctly notes that even accepting Craig's framework on its own terms (which he personally rejects as insufficiently grounded in original meaning), Mississippi's mandatory statute fails because Craig explicitly requires case-specific judicial findings, not legislative presumptions. The strongest argument for the Respondent would be harmless error — the independent evidence of guilt was substantial — but as Justice Kavanaugh rightly observes, this cannot cure a structural departure from a constitutionally mandated procedural requirement, and more fundamentally, the trial court never conducted the individualized inquiry at all, so we cannot know what a proper hearing would have produced. Mississippi stands as a singular outlier defying controlling precedent, the trial judge himself expressed constitutional doubt yet felt mechanically bound, and the factual record — a four-year-old expressing affection for the defendant — affirmatively undermines the very necessity the statute presumes.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself speaks to how clear-cut this constitutional violation is. Justice Thomas's point is particularly notable — even he, who would go further than Craig and find no exceptions to face-to-face confrontation whatsoever, recognizes that Mississippi's statute fails even under Craig's more permissive framework. The strongest argument for the Respondent would be harmless error — the child's age, the independent evidence of guilt, and the protective purposes of the statute — but as Justice Kagan correctly identifies, the structural nature of this violation, flowing from a mandatory legislative override of a constitutionally required judicial determination, cannot be cured by post-hoc sufficiency analysis. The trial judge's own expressed constitutional doubt, combined with the child's affirmative expression of affection for the defendant, makes this not merely a technical Craig violation but a case where the factual record affirmatively contradicts the very necessity the statute presumes, and Mississippi's status as a singular outlier defying controlling precedent demands reversal to preserve the uniform application of Sixth Amendment rights.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself is telling — when Justice Thomas and Justice Sotomayor reach the same conclusion through different methodological paths, the constitutional answer is usually clear. The strongest argument the State could marshal is harmless error given the independent evidence of guilt, but as Justice Alito correctly notes, the failure to conduct the individualized Craig inquiry is not merely a trial error susceptible to harmless error analysis — it is a structural failure to satisfy a constitutionally mandated procedural prerequisite, and we cannot permit states to bypass that requirement simply because the underlying evidence may have been sufficient. Justice Barrett's point about the factual record is particularly devastating: when the very child witness the statute presumes will be traumatized by confrontation instead expresses affection for the defendant, the mandatory legislative presumption is not just procedurally defective but empirically refuted on these specific facts. Mississippi stands as a singular outlier defying Craig's clear holding, and the institutional integrity of this Court's constitutional jurisprudence requires that we correct the Mississippi Supreme Court's error.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself is telling — when Justice Thomas and Justice Sotomayor reach the same conclusion through their respective methodologies, the constitutional answer is clear. Justice Thomas correctly notes that even accepting Craig's framework on its own terms (which he personally rejects as insufficiently grounded in original meaning), Mississippi's mandatory statute fails because Craig explicitly requires case-specific judicial findings, not legislative presumptions. The strongest argument for the Respondent would be a harmless error claim given the independent evidence of guilt, but as Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson persuasively argue, the structural nature of this violation — a legislature categorically stripping courts of their constitutionally mandated fact-finding obligation — cannot be cured by post-hoc sufficiency analysis. The trial judge's own expressed constitutional doubts, combined with the child's affirmative expression of affection for the defendant, make this record particularly unsuitable for harmless error treatment, and Mississippi's status as a universal outlier among all jurisdictions confirms that the Mississippi Supreme Court's ruling cannot stand.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with Chief Justice Roberts's framing that this is not a close case — the mandatory nature of Mississippi Code § 99-43-101(2)(g) removes precisely the individualized judicial inquiry that Craig demands, and the trial judge's own expressed constitutional doubts while feeling mechanically bound by the statute is the clearest possible evidence that no case-specific necessity finding was made. Justice Thomas raises an interesting point about Craig's framework from his original dissenting position, but even accepting his view that Craig was wrongly decided, the result here is the same: the Confrontation Clause was violated. The strongest argument for the Respondent — harmless error given the independent evidence of guilt — is addressed most directly by Justice Jackson's observation that the structural nature of this violation, flowing from a mandatory legislative override of a constitutionally required judicial process, counsels against harmless error analysis; I would add that permitting harmless error to cure the complete absence of the required Craig inquiry would effectively nullify Craig's individualized-finding requirement whenever the underlying evidence of guilt is strong. Mississippi's status as a singular outlier defying controlling precedent that every other jurisdiction follows is itself an institutional concern that reinforces the merits analysis.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself is telling — when Justice Thomas (who would go further and eliminate Craig's exceptions entirely) and Justice Sotomayor (who emphasizes child protection interests) reach the same conclusion, the constitutional analysis is on firm ground. Justice Kagan's framing of the structural nature of the violation is particularly apt: this is not a case where we must weigh competing considerations, but rather one where a mandatory legislative presumption has categorically displaced the individualized judicial inquiry that Craig explicitly requires. The strongest argument for the Respondent — that the State has compelling child-protection interests and that the evidence of guilt was overwhelming — fails under Craig's framework because harmless error analysis cannot cure the threshold failure to conduct the required case-specific necessity finding, especially where the factual record (the child's expressed affection for the defendant) affirmatively negates the presumed necessity. Mississippi's statute is constitutionally defective on its face as applied here, and the trial court's own expressed constitutional reservations confirm that the mandatory language prevented any genuine individualized inquiry — the precise evil Coy identified when it rejected Iowa's analogous legislative screen.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I am in full agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, and I find Justice Thomas's observation particularly notable — that even he, who would go further than Craig and find no exceptions to face-to-face confrontation, recognizes that Mississippi's mandatory statute fails even under Craig's more permissive framework. The strongest argument for the Respondent would be harmless error — that the independent evidence of guilt was so overwhelming that any Confrontation Clause violation was inconsequential — but as Justice Kagan correctly notes, the violation here is structural in character because it flows from a mandatory legislative override of a constitutionally required judicial-finding process, not merely an erroneous evidentiary ruling. My background as a public defender reinforces my conviction that procedural fairness is not a technicality to be traded away when the evidence seems strong; the constitutional guarantee of confrontation exists precisely to test the reliability of evidence that appears compelling, and mechanical application of a legislative presumption without individualized inquiry corrupts that testing function at its root. The trial judge's own expressed constitutional doubts, combined with the child's affirmative expression of affection for the defendant, make this record as damning as any I could imagine for a harmless error argument, and Mississippi's status as a singular outlier defying controlling precedent demands reversal.

John Roberts.reasoning: The controlling precedents of Coy v. Iowa and Maryland v. Craig establish a clear constitutional requirement that before a trial court may depart from face-to-face confrontation, it must make an individualized, case-specific finding of necessity — a legislative presumption of trauma cannot substitute for that judicial determination. Mississippi Code § 99-43-101(2)(g) is facially incompatible with this requirement because it mandates use of the screen procedure without requiring any individualized judicial inquiry, and the record here is particularly damning: the trial judge himself expressed constitutional doubts yet felt bound by the mandatory statute, and the child witness affirmatively expressed love for the defendant, directly undermining any presumption of necessity. While I am generally reluctant to disturb state court judgments and prefer narrow rulings, this is not a close case — the Mississippi Supreme Court has placed itself in direct conflict with controlling federal constitutional precedent that every other jurisdiction follows, and institutional legitimacy demands that state courts not be permitted to simply disregard this Court's clear holdings. I would reverse on the narrowest possible ground — that the mandatory statutory procedure without individualized findings violates Craig — and remand without prejudging whether a properly conducted hearing might support use of the screen on these specific facts.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause's text and original public meaning guarantee a defendant the right to face-to-face confrontation with witnesses against him, and while I wrote in dissent in Maryland v. Craig that the Clause admits no exceptions whatsoever to this requirement, even accepting Craig's framework on its own terms, Mississippi's mandatory statute plainly violates it. Craig explicitly requires a case-specific, individualized judicial finding of necessity before face-to-face confrontation may be dispensed with — a legislatively imposed presumption of trauma is constitutionally insufficient, as Coy v. Iowa made clear in 1988. Here, the trial court itself expressed constitutional doubt about the statute yet felt mechanically bound by its mandatory language, making no individualized finding — indeed, the factual record affirmatively undermined any necessity finding, as the four-year-old child expressed affection for the defendant rather than fear. Mississippi stands alone among all jurisdictions in defying this controlling precedent, and state courts are bound by this Court's Sixth Amendment interpretations under the Supremacy Clause, as Hicks v. Miranda and Czekala-Chatham confirm.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As a textualist who takes seriously the actual requirements established by this Court's precedents, I cannot ignore that Maryland v. Craig, 497 U.S. 836 (1990), explicitly requires a case-specific, individualized judicial finding of necessity before a trial court may depart from face-to-face confrontation — and Mississippi Code § 99-43-101(2)(g) substitutes a legislative presumption for that required judicial determination, which is precisely what Coy v. Iowa, 487 U.S. 1012 (1988), forbade. The trial court here acknowledged constitutional concerns yet mechanically applied the mandatory statute without conducting the individualized inquiry Craig demands, and the factual record — including the child's expressed affection for the defendant — affirmatively undermines any presumption of trauma-based necessity. While I am generally skeptical of expansive readings of defendants' rights and sympathetic to law enforcement and child protection interests, the Confrontation Clause's requirements as articulated in Craig are clear, binding, and were plainly violated; state legislatures cannot override this Court's constitutional holdings through mandatory statutes, regardless of how well-intentioned those statutes may be. The harmless error argument is insufficient to excuse the structural failure to conduct the required individualized finding in the first instance.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Maryland v. Craig, 497 U.S. 836 (1990), a trial court may only dispense with face-to-face confrontation after making a case-specific, individualized finding of necessity — a legislative presumption of trauma categorically cannot substitute for that judicial determination, as Coy v. Iowa, 487 U.S. 1012 (1988), made clear when it struck down a nearly identical screen procedure imposed without individualized findings. Mississippi Code § 99-43-101(2)(g) is facially unconstitutional as applied here because it mandates the screen procedure without requiring any individualized judicial inquiry, and the trial court itself expressed constitutional doubt yet felt bound by the statute's mandatory language — precisely the mechanical application Craig forbids. The factual record here is particularly damning: the four-year-old child expressed affection for her father and showed no observable signs of trauma from his presence, which directly contradicts any presumed necessity and underscores why individualized findings are constitutionally indispensable. While I am deeply committed to protecting child witnesses from genuine trauma, the Constitution's confrontation guarantee cannot be overridden by legislative fiat, and Mississippi stands as a singular outlier among all jurisdictions in refusing to follow controlling Supreme Court precedent.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Maryland v. Craig is unambiguous: before a trial court may depart from face-to-face confrontation, it must make a case-specific, individualized finding of necessity — a legislative presumption of trauma categorically cannot substitute for that judicial determination. Mississippi Code § 99-43-101(2)(g) does precisely what Craig forbids by mandating the screen procedure without requiring any individualized judicial inquiry, and the trial judge's own expressed constitutional reservations confirm the statute was applied mechanically rather than through the required case-specific analysis. The factual record here is particularly damning: the four-year-old child expressed affection toward the defendant, providing no evidentiary basis whatsoever for a necessity finding even had one been attempted. While I take seriously the State's harmless error argument given the independent evidence of guilt, the Confrontation Clause violation here is structural in the sense that it flows from a mandatory legislative override of a constitutional judicial-finding requirement, and the Mississippi Supreme Court's endorsement of this approach creates a direct, acknowledged conflict with controlling federal precedent that this Court cannot leave standing.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The text of the Sixth Amendment guarantees the accused the right 'to be confronted with the witnesses against him,' and this Court's precedents in Coy v. Iowa and Maryland v. Craig have given that text concrete meaning: before a trial court may depart from face-to-face confrontation, it must make an individualized, case-specific finding that the procedure is necessary to protect the particular witness from trauma. Mississippi Code § 99-43-101(2)(g) is a mandatory categorical statute that substitutes a legislative presumption of trauma for the constitutionally required judicial fact-finding — precisely the kind of legislative override that Coy explicitly rejected. The factual record here makes the constitutional violation especially stark: the child expressed affection for the defendant, the trial judge himself voiced constitutional doubts, and yet felt mechanically bound by the statute's mandatory language, which is the antithesis of the individualized inquiry Craig demands. A state legislature cannot, consistent with the Supremacy Clause and this Court's binding precedent, strip trial courts of their obligation to make case-specific necessity findings by enacting a mandatory victim-protection statute, however well-intentioned, and the Mississippi Supreme Court erred in holding otherwise.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Maryland v. Craig and Coy v. Iowa establish a clear, binding constitutional rule that before a trial court may depart from face-to-face confrontation, it must make a case-specific, individualized finding of necessity — a legislative presumption of trauma cannot substitute for that judicial determination. Mississippi's mandatory statute under § 99-43-101(2)(g) does precisely what Craig forbids: it removes the individualized judicial inquiry entirely and replaces it with a categorical legislative presumption, which the trial judge himself recognized as constitutionally suspect. The factual record here is particularly damning for the State's position — the child witness expressed affection for the defendant, providing no evidentiary basis whatsoever for a necessity finding even had one been attempted. As an institutionalist, I am deeply concerned that allowing Mississippi to stand as the sole outlier jurisdiction defying controlling Supreme Court precedent would undermine the Court's authority and the uniform application of constitutional rights, and the harmless error argument, while not frivolous given the independent evidence, cannot cure a structural departure from a constitutionally mandated procedural requirement.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text and original public meaning of the Sixth Amendment's Confrontation Clause, as authoritatively construed in Coy v. Iowa and Maryland v. Craig, requires a case-specific, individualized judicial finding of necessity before a trial court may depart from face-to-face confrontation — a legislative presumption categorically cannot substitute for that judicial determination. Mississippi Code § 99-43-101(2)(g) is constitutionally defective precisely because it mandates the screen procedure without requiring any individualized finding, and the trial court's own expressed constitutional reservations confirm that no such finding was made here. The factual record is particularly damning: the four-year-old child expressed affection toward the defendant, directly negating any presumption of trauma-inducing necessity, which is the very evil Coy identified when it rejected Iowa's analogous legislative presumption. Under Maryland v. Craig, the necessity finding 'must of course be a case-specific one' supported by evidence heard by the trial court — a requirement the Mississippi Supreme Court's decision openly defies, making it an outlier among every federal circuit and state supreme court that has addressed this question.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Maryland v. Craig, 497 U.S. 836 (1990), and Coy v. Iowa, 487 U.S. 1012 (1988), a trial court may dispense with face-to-face confrontation only upon a case-specific, individualized finding of necessity — a legislatively mandated presumption of trauma categorically cannot substitute for that judicial determination. Mississippi Code Section 99-43-101(2)(g)'s mandatory application of the screen procedure without requiring individualized judicial fact-finding is precisely the kind of legislative presumption that Coy explicitly rejected, and the trial judge's own expressed constitutional concerns about the statute underscore that no genuine case-specific inquiry was conducted. The factual record here is particularly damning: the four-year-old witness expressed affection for the defendant, directly contradicting any presumed necessity, yet the screen was applied mechanically — the antithesis of what Craig demands. As for harmless error, while the State's evidence may be substantial, the structural nature of this Confrontation Clause violation and Mississippi's status as a clear outlier among all jurisdictions that have addressed this question counsel strongly against finding the error harmless, as procedural fairness and the integrity of the constitutional guarantee require reversal.

case_analysis.petitioner_position: The trial court failed to make the individualized, case-specific finding required by Coy v. Iowa and Maryland v. Craig before departing from face-to-face confrontation; instead, it mechanically applied a mandatory state statute that presumes trauma for all child witnesses, which is constitutionally impermissible. Critically, the actual trial evidence showed the child was excited — not traumatized — to see her father, and the trial judge himself expressed concern about the statute's constitutionality but felt he lacked discretion to deviate from it. Petitioner argues summary reversal is appropriate given the clear conflict with controlling Supreme Court precedent.

The trial court adequately determined the screen procedure was necessary to protect the child from trauma, and the determination was supported by guardian testimony and other evidence presented at the tender-years hearing. Additionally, overwhelming independent evidence of guilt — including witness testimony, statements to authorities, and a videotaped forensic interview — renders any Confrontation Clause error harmless beyond a reasonable doubt.

case_analysis.legal_complexity: Complex — The case sits at the intersection of constitutional Confrontation Clause doctrine, mandatory state statutory procedure, child witness protection policy, harmless error analysis, and the binding authority of federal precedent on state courts. It raises unresolved tension between legislative presumptions of child witness trauma and the constitutionally mandated individualized judicial inquiry, implicating both structural separation-of-powers concerns and fundamental trial rights.

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference is remarkably unified, and I find my colleagues' reasoning persuasive precisely because it converges on the narrow, controlling ground I would emphasize: Maryland v. Craig's case-specific finding requirement is not ambiguous, and Mississippi's mandatory statute categorically bypasses it. Justice Kavanaugh correctly identifies that the Mississippi Supreme Court's reliance on the state Crime Victim Rights Amendment cannot override binding federal constitutional precedent under the Supremacy Clause — that is the cleanest basis for reversal and avoids any need to revisit Craig's underlying framework. I note Justice Thomas's invitation to question Craig's balancing approach on originalist grounds, but as a minimalist I would firmly decline that path; we need not disturb Craig to resolve this case, and doing so would unnecessarily unsettle settled doctrine across dozens of jurisdictions. My preferred opinion would be narrow: Mississippi's mandatory statute, as applied without any individualized judicial finding — and against a record showing the child was excited rather than traumatized — violates Craig, with the question of harmless error remanded for proper analysis by the lower courts.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: My colleagues have presented a unified and compelling case, and I find myself in substantial agreement with Justice Gorsuch's originalist framing, which most closely tracks my own methodology. The Confrontation Clause's text and original public meaning, as illuminated by Coy v. Iowa, strongly suggest that face-to-face confrontation was understood as a near-absolute right — and while I continue to harbor serious doubts about Craig's balancing framework as a matter of original meaning (as Justice Scalia's dissent persuasively argued), Craig at minimum demands what Mississippi plainly failed to provide: a case-specific, individualized judicial finding of necessity. The strongest argument for the respondent — that the State has a compelling interest in protecting child witnesses and that the forensic interview and other evidence render any error harmless — fails because Craig's requirement is not merely procedural window-dressing but a constitutional floor below which no legislative presumption may descend, and the record's affirmative evidence that the child was excited rather than traumatized to see her father makes any harmless error argument particularly difficult to sustain. Mississippi's mandatory statute stands as a direct repudiation of this Court's binding precedent, and under the Supremacy Clause, state courts and legislatures cannot substitute categorical legislative judgments for the individualized judicial inquiry the Constitution demands.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: My colleagues have collectively and persuasively reinforced what I already recognized as the controlling principle: Maryland v. Craig demands an individualized, case-specific judicial finding of necessity, and Mississippi's mandatory statute categorically fails that requirement. Justice Thomas raises an interesting originalist point about whether Craig's balancing framework itself strains the Confrontation Clause's original meaning — a concern I find intellectually serious — but even accepting Craig as binding precedent, as we all must, Mississippi's scheme is plainly unconstitutional. The strongest argument for the respondent would be harmless error, and Justice Sotomayor's point that courts should be cautious about finding harmlessness when a core confrontation right has been systematically violated resonates with me, though I remain open to a more searching harmless error analysis on remand rather than categorical rejection of that doctrine here. The unanimity of my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, combined with the damning record fact that the child was excited rather than traumatized to see her father, confirms that this is not a close case on the Craig violation itself.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I find myself in complete agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself speaks to the clarity of Craig's mandate. Justice Jackson's point resonates most deeply with me — as someone who has always insisted that constitutional rights must be real and not merely formal, the fact that a mandatory statute stripped the trial judge of the very discretion Craig requires is not a technical defect but a structural one that strikes at the heart of the adversarial system. Justice Alito raises the most serious counterargument by noting the harmless error question is 'closer' given the forensic interview and corroborating evidence, but I cannot accept that harmless error analysis should readily cure what is essentially a categorical legislative override of a constitutionally mandated judicial procedure — the Confrontation Clause's individualized inquiry requirement exists precisely because we cannot know in advance which cases turn on credibility assessments that face-to-face confrontation might affect. The record's most damning fact — that the child was excited, not traumatized, to see her father — means this is not even a close case on the merits of necessity, and Mississippi's outlier status among all jurisdictions confirms that Craig's requirements are both workable and constitutionally compelled.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: My colleagues have collectively and persuasively converged on the core constitutional defect, and I find the analysis sound from my pragmatic textualist perspective. Justice Roberts correctly identifies the minimalist path: we need not reach broad questions about Craig's framework itself — we simply apply Craig's unambiguous requirement that individualized judicial fact-finding precede any departure from face-to-face confrontation, and Mississippi's mandatory statute categorically fails that test. Justice Thomas raises an interesting originalist challenge to Craig's balancing framework itself, but as he acknowledges, Craig remains binding precedent and Mississippi fails even under Craig's more permissive standard. The strongest argument for the State — harmless error given the forensic interview and corroborating evidence — is real but ultimately unavailing because, as Justice Sotomayor notes, the constitutional violation here operates at the structural level of the proceeding: when a mandatory statute strips the trial court of the very discretion Craig requires it to exercise, we cannot retroactively reconstruct a necessity finding from evidence the court never properly weighed for that purpose, and the child's reported excitement at seeing her father makes any such reconstruction particularly implausible.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: I am in full agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, and the unanimity here reflects how clearly Craig controls this case. Justice Thomas raises the most intellectually honest point — that Craig's balancing framework itself strains the original meaning of the Confrontation Clause, as Justice Scalia's Craig dissent powerfully argued — but even accepting Craig as binding precedent, Mississippi's mandatory statute fails on its own terms by substituting a legislative presumption for the individualized judicial finding Craig expressly requires. The strongest argument for the respondent would be harmless error, and I take seriously Justice Alito's acknowledgment that the question is 'closer' given the forensic interview and corroborating evidence, but I cannot accept that harmless error analysis applies when the constitutional violation is structural — the trial court never initiated the constitutionally required procedure at all, and a defendant's right to face his accuser cannot be deemed harmlessly violated when the record affirmatively shows the child was excited rather than traumatized by his presence. Mississippi stands as a singular outlier in defying settled federal constitutional precedent, and the Supremacy Clause demands we correct that.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with Chief Justice Roberts's minimalist framing and Justice Barrett's observation that Mississippi stands as a categorical outlier against every federal circuit and state court that has addressed this question — both points reinforce that this is not a close case under Craig. The strongest argument for the respondent would be harmless error given the forensic interview and corroborating evidence, but as Justice Kagan correctly notes, Craig's individualized necessity requirement functions as a procedural safeguard that cannot be bypassed by legislative mandate and then retroactively validated by sufficiency of other evidence. The constitutional defect here is structural: a mandatory statute that removes judicial discretion and presumes trauma for an entire class of witnesses is categorically incompatible with Craig's demand for case-specific findings, and the trial judge's own expressed constitutional discomfort while feeling bound by the statute is perhaps the most damning evidence that the required inquiry never occurred. I would reverse and remand on the narrow Craig ground, leaving open whether a properly conducted individualized hearing might satisfy constitutional requirements on remand.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: My colleagues have collectively and persuasively reinforced the core constitutional deficiency here, and I find the conference remarkably unified on the controlling principle. Justice Thomas raises an interesting methodological point — that Craig's balancing framework itself may strain the original public meaning of the Confrontation Clause, as Justice Scalia argued in dissent — but even accepting Craig as binding precedent (which it is), Mississippi's mandatory statute fails on Craig's own terms because it substitutes a categorical legislative presumption for the individualized judicial finding Craig explicitly requires. Justice Gorsuch's emphasis on the structural nature of the violation resonates with my textualist methodology: the Confrontation Clause's guarantee is not merely a procedural nicety but a structural safeguard, and when a mandatory statute eliminates the constitutionally required judicial inquiry altogether, no quantum of independent evidence can retroactively supply the missing necessity determination. The strongest argument for the respondent — harmless error given the forensic interview and corroborating evidence — has some force, but as Justice Sotomayor correctly notes, courts should be cautious about finding harmlessness when a core confrontation right has been systematically violated through a mechanism that threatens defendants beyond this single case.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I find myself in strong agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, and I want to engage directly with the strongest counterargument the respondent could raise — that the independent evidence of guilt (the forensic interview, corroborating physical evidence) renders any constitutional error harmless. Justice Alito correctly notes this is the closest question, but as I emphasized in my initial reasoning and as Justice Sotomayor articulates with particular force, the Confrontation Clause violation here is not merely evidentiary but structural: a mandatory statute that categorically strips the trial court of its constitutionally required role as individualized fact-finder cannot be cured by asking whether the jury would have convicted anyway on other evidence. My background as a public defender compels me to underscore what Justice Gorsuch captures from a different methodological direction — that the very mechanism of the error, a legislature presuming away a constitutional right for an entire class of defendants, represents a systemic threat that harmless error analysis is ill-suited to address. The trial judge's own expressed doubt, combined with the affirmative evidence that the child was excited rather than traumatized to see her father, makes this not merely a procedural defect but a case where the factual predicate for the exception was actively contradicted, and I would reverse and remand for a properly conducted Craig hearing.

John Roberts.reasoning: Maryland v. Craig is unambiguous: before departing from face-to-face confrontation, a trial court must make a case-specific, individualized finding of necessity — a legislative presumption of trauma categorically cannot substitute for that judicial inquiry. Here, the trial court itself expressed constitutional doubt about the mandatory statute yet felt compelled to apply it mechanically, which is precisely the kind of legislative override of judicial constitutional obligation that Craig forbids. The record is particularly damaging to the State's position because the actual evidence showed the child was excited rather than traumatized by her father's presence, meaning not only was no individualized finding made, but the available evidence affirmatively cut against necessity. As a minimalist, I would resolve this on the narrow ground that Mississippi's mandatory statutory scheme, as applied here without any case-specific judicial finding, conflicts directly with controlling federal precedent binding on all state courts under the Supremacy Clause, and I would leave open whether a properly conducted hearing on remand might satisfy Craig's requirements.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Sixth Amendment's Confrontation Clause, as interpreted through its original public meaning and reinforced by Coy v. Iowa and Maryland v. Craig, demands that any departure from face-to-face confrontation be predicated upon an individualized, case-specific judicial finding of necessity — not a legislative presumption applicable to an entire class of witnesses. Mississippi's mandatory statute, Miss. Code § 99-43-101(2)(g), unconstitutionally substitutes a categorical legislative judgment for the constitutionally required individualized inquiry, and the trial judge himself acknowledged he lacked discretion to deviate from the statute despite harboring constitutional doubts. The record here is particularly damning: the child witness was reportedly excited — not traumatized — to see the defendant, which directly undermines any finding of necessity and illustrates precisely why Craig demands case-specific findings rather than blanket presumptions. While I write separately to note that Craig's balancing framework itself strains the original meaning of the Confrontation Clause — as Justice Scalia's dissent in Craig persuasively argued that face-to-face confrontation admits of no exceptions — the majority rule in Craig at minimum requires what Mississippi plainly failed to provide here, and state courts remain bound by this Court's precedent under Hicks v. Miranda.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As a textualist, I must apply the controlling precedent of Maryland v. Craig, 497 U.S. 836 (1990), which unambiguously requires a case-specific, individualized judicial finding of necessity before departing from the Confrontation Clause's face-to-face requirement — a legislative presumption of trauma categorically cannot substitute for that judicial inquiry. Mississippi Code § 99-43-101(2)(g) is constitutionally defective precisely because it mandates the screen procedure without requiring the trial court to make the individualized finding Craig demands, and the record here is particularly damning: the trial judge himself expressed constitutional doubts yet felt bound by the statute, and the actual evidence showed the child was excited rather than traumatized by her father's presence. While I am generally skeptical of expansive readings that hamper law enforcement, the Confrontation Clause's text and Craig's clear doctrinal rule leave no room for a mandatory legislative presumption to override the constitutionally required judicial determination, and Mississippi stands alone among all jurisdictions in defying this settled precedent. On harmless error, the question is closer given the forensic interview and other independent evidence, but the constitutional violation at the structural level of the proceeding warrants reversal and remand for proper analysis.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Maryland v. Craig explicitly requires a case-specific, individualized finding of necessity before a trial court may depart from face-to-face confrontation, and Mississippi's mandatory statute categorically substitutes a legislative presumption of trauma for that constitutionally required judicial inquiry — precisely what Craig forbids. The record here is particularly damning: the trial judge himself expressed constitutional doubt about the statute yet felt compelled to apply it mechanically, and the actual evidence before the court showed the child was excited rather than traumatized to see the defendant, which is the antithesis of the necessity finding Craig demands. While I am deeply sympathetic to the state's interest in protecting child witnesses from trauma — an interest I take seriously — the Constitution requires that protection be grounded in individualized evidence, not legislative presumption, because the Confrontation Clause's guarantee is a structural safeguard against wrongful conviction that protects the most vulnerable defendants as well as the most vulnerable witnesses. As for harmless error, the presence of other evidence does not cure the constitutional defect at the trial court level where no valid necessity finding was ever made, and courts should be cautious about too readily finding harmlessness when a core confrontation right has been systematically violated.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The constitutional requirement established in Maryland v. Craig is unambiguous: before departing from face-to-face confrontation, a trial court must make a case-specific, individualized finding of necessity — not merely apply a legislative presumption that all child witnesses in sexual abuse cases will suffer trauma. Mississippi's mandatory statute, Miss. Code § 99-43-101(2)(g), impermissibly substitutes a categorical legislative judgment for the constitutionally required judicial inquiry, and the trial record here is particularly damning: the judge himself expressed constitutional reservations yet felt bound by the statute, and the actual evidence showed the child was excited rather than traumatized to see her father. As a pragmatic textualist, I take seriously the State's interest in protecting child witnesses, and Craig itself accommodates that interest — but only through the procedural safeguard of individualized judicial fact-finding, which is precisely what was bypassed here. The harmless error argument, while not frivolous given the forensic interview and corroborating evidence, cannot cure a structural departure from a constitutionally mandated procedural requirement that the Court has consistently treated as essential to Confrontation Clause integrity.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Confrontation Clause's text and original meaning, as illuminated by Coy v. Iowa and Maryland v. Craig, demand an individualized, case-specific judicial finding before face-to-face confrontation may be denied — a legislative presumption of trauma categorically cannot substitute for that constitutionally mandated inquiry. Mississippi's mandatory statute, Miss. Code § 99-43-101(2)(g), does precisely what Craig forbids: it transfers the necessity determination from the trial judge to the legislature, eliminating the case-specific finding altogether. The record here is particularly damning — the trial judge himself expressed constitutional doubt about the statute yet felt compelled to apply it mechanically, and the actual evidence showed the child was excited rather than traumatized by her father's presence, the very antithesis of the necessity Craig requires. As Justice Scalia's Coy majority recognized, few constitutional violations are more 'obvious or damaging' than deliberately blocking a defendant's face-to-face encounter with his accuser, and the harmless error argument cannot rescue a structural departure from a constitutional procedure that was never properly initiated in the first place.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Maryland v. Craig is controlling and unambiguous: before departing from the Confrontation Clause's face-to-face requirement, a trial court must make a case-specific, individualized finding of necessity — a legislative presumption of trauma categorically cannot substitute for that judicial inquiry. Mississippi's mandatory statute, Miss. Code § 99-43-101(2)(g), does precisely what Craig forbids by removing judicial discretion and presuming necessity for all child witnesses, and the trial judge himself acknowledged his constitutional discomfort while feeling bound by the statute. The facts here are particularly stark: the child was reportedly excited — not traumatized — to see the defendant, which is the antithesis of the evidentiary showing Craig demands, and the Mississippi Supreme Court's deference to the state constitutional Crime Victim Rights Amendment cannot override binding federal constitutional precedent under the Supremacy Clause. While I take seriously the respondent's harmless error argument given the substantial independent evidence, the structural constitutional violation — a mandatory statute displacing the required individualized judicial finding — warrants reversal and remand rather than affirmance, as institutional respect for this Court's precedent demands that state courts not be permitted to circumvent Craig through legislative mandate.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under Maryland v. Craig, 497 U.S. 836 (1990), the Confrontation Clause permits dispensing with face-to-face confrontation only upon a case-specific, individualized judicial finding that the particular child witness would suffer trauma from the defendant's presence — a legislative presumption of trauma categorically cannot substitute for this constitutionally mandated inquiry. Here, the trial court did not make such an individualized finding; it mechanically applied Mississippi Code § 99-43-101(2)(g), a mandatory statute that presumes trauma for all child witnesses in sexual abuse cases, which is precisely the kind of categorical legislative determination Craig forbids. The constitutional deficiency is compounded by the trial record itself, which showed the child was excited — not traumatized — to see her father, and by the trial judge's own expressed doubt about his discretion to deviate from the statute, confirming that no genuine case-specific necessity determination was made. While the respondent's harmless error argument has some force given the independent evidence of guilt, the structural constitutional violation — a mandatory statute overriding the individualized judicial inquiry Craig requires — warrants reversal and remand rather than affirmance, as Mississippi's rule stands as a direct outlier against every federal circuit and state supreme court that has addressed this question.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Maryland v. Craig, 497 U.S. 836 (1990), a trial court may dispense with face-to-face confrontation only upon a case-specific, individualized finding of necessity — a legislative presumption of trauma cannot substitute for that judicial inquiry. Here, the trial court mechanically applied Mississippi Code Section 99-43-101(2)(g), a mandatory statute that presumes trauma for all child witnesses in sexual abuse cases, without making the constitutionally required individualized determination. This is constitutionally fatal: the trial judge himself expressed doubt about the statute's constitutionality yet felt bound to apply it, and critically, the actual trial evidence showed the child was excited — not traumatized — to see her father, directly undermining any presumption of necessity. While the respondent urges harmless error given the independent evidence of guilt, I cannot lightly dismiss a structural Confrontation Clause violation of this magnitude, particularly where the very mechanism of the error — a mandatory statute that strips judicial discretion — represents a systemic threat to defendants' constitutional rights that my background as a public defender compels me to take seriously.
